column1: Young man following a motor vehicle crash Q01M7X9K2P4Z
column5:
Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture

Keyword findings:
• pneumothorax
• chest tube
• nasogastric (NG) tube
• curved up toward the chest

In trauma, an abnormally high or distorted hemidiaphragm with an NG tube coursing upward into the chest is a classic radiographic clue to diaphragmatic rupture with intrathoracic stomach.

Differential:
Diaphragmatic eventration
Diaphragmatic paralysis
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Pleural effusion or pulmonary/extrapleural mass
column21:
🧭 Traumatic Diaphragmatic Rupture
Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture is disruption of the diaphragm, with or without herniation of abdominal contents into the thorax. Recognition depends on direct diaphragmatic discontinuity and secondary displacement of abdominal viscera, especially on multiplanar contrast-enhanced CT.
Source Basis: RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis (Core GAP)

📖 Summary
  • Synonym: traumatic diaphragmatic hernia.
  • About 75% result from blunt trauma and 25% from penetrating trauma.
  • Most injuries are left-sided (RadPrimer: 90-98%), usually posterolateral and medial to the spleen.
  • Blunt tears are usually large, often >10 cm; stab wounds usually create shorter 1-2 cm lacerations and are more likely to be delayed or missed.
🔍 Key Imaging Findings
  • CT: focal/discontinuous hemidiaphragm defect, dangling diaphragm, absent diaphragm, organ herniation, collar sign, and fallen/dependent viscus sign.
  • Secondary CT clues: pneumothorax with pneumoperitoneum, hemothorax with hemoperitoneum, active extravasation near the diaphragm, asymmetric elevation, nearby organ injury, pleural fluid tracking into the upper abdomen, or contiguous injury above and below the diaphragm.
  • Best imaging tool: contrast-enhanced CT with multiplanar reformations; coronal/sagittal reformats are important because the diaphragm may lie parallel to the axial plane.
  • Radiography: elevated or nonvisualized hemidiaphragm, intrathoracic soft tissue/gas or air-fluid levels, mediastinal shift, ipsilateral thoracic injury, or a high NG tube. An NG tube above the left hemidiaphragm with an abnormal U-shaped course or tip toward the left shoulder is a classic clue.
  • MRI: the diaphragm is a continuous low-signal band on T1- and T2-weighted imaging; MR signs parallel CT and MRI is generally reserved for stable patients.
  • Fluoroscopy: upper GI or barium enema may show a collar sign in delayed hernia but is rarely needed acutely.
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Congenital Bochdalek or Morgagni hernia: lacks trauma history and adjacent traumatic secondary signs.
  • Diaphragmatic eventration: thinned but continuous diaphragm remains attached to the costal margin; no focal defect, collar sign, or fallen viscus sign.
  • Paralyzed diaphragm: elevated but intact diaphragm without focal tear or herniation signs.
  • Pleural effusion or pulmonary/extrapleural mass may mimic the appearance on radiographs but should separate on CT.
🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Lateral blunt impact produces shear injury; frontal impact raises intraabdominal pressure and can rupture the diaphragm.
  • Diaphragmatic injuries do not heal spontaneously because of constant motion and the pressure gradient across the diaphragm.
  • If abdominal contents do not herniate immediately, negative intrapleural pressure can promote later herniation; positive-pressure ventilation may temporarily mask it.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Always inspect the diaphragm on trauma CT, especially when more obvious visceral injuries are present.
  • Right-sided injuries are more likely to be missed.
  • Contusion, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, atelectasis, and phrenic nerve palsy can obscure the injury.
  • Complications include obstruction or ischemia of herniated bowel, ischemia of herniated solid organs, respiratory compromise, and central venous obstruction; STATdx also describes tension gastrothorax.
📊 Key Measurements / Outcomes
  • Reported CT sensitivity may be as low as 73% and specificity as low as 50%.
  • Diaphragmatic injuries are missed in 7-66% of cases.
  • Associated injuries are reported in 52-100% of cases.
  • Overall mortality is reported by RadPrimer at 12-42%, largely from associated severe injuries; STATdx reports 30-60% mortality with delayed diagnosis and repair.
⭐ Super Summary
  • In trauma, think diaphragmatic rupture when abdominal viscera or fat are abnormally intrathoracic, especially with a collar sign, fallen/dependent viscus sign, or a focal diaphragm defect.
  • Use multiplanar CECT aggressively, and treat injuries above and below the diaphragm as a warning pattern even if the tear itself is subtle.

Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture is disruption of the diaphragm, with or without herniation of abdominal contents into the thorax. Recognition depends on direct diaphragmatic discontinuity and secondary displacement of abdominal viscera, especially on multiplanar contrast-enhanced CT.
Source Basis: RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis (Core GAP)

📖 Summary
  • Synonym: traumatic diaphragmatic hernia.
  • About 75% result from blunt trauma and 25% from penetrating trauma.
  • Most injuries are left-sided (RadPrimer: 90-98%), usually posterolateral and medial to the spleen.
  • Blunt tears are usually large, often >10 cm; stab wounds usually create shorter 1-2 cm lacerations and are more likely to be delayed or missed.
🔍 Key Imaging Findings
  • CT: focal/discontinuous hemidiaphragm defect, dangling diaphragm, absent diaphragm, organ herniation, collar sign, and fallen/dependent viscus sign.
  • Secondary CT clues: pneumothorax with pneumoperitoneum, hemothorax with hemoperitoneum, active extravasation near the diaphragm, asymmetric elevation, nearby organ injury, pleural fluid tracking into the upper abdomen, or contiguous injury above and below the diaphragm.
  • Best imaging tool: contrast-enhanced CT with multiplanar reformations; coronal/sagittal reformats are important because the diaphragm may lie parallel to the axial plane.
  • Radiography: elevated or nonvisualized hemidiaphragm, intrathoracic soft tissue/gas or air-fluid levels, mediastinal shift, ipsilateral thoracic injury, or a high NG tube. An NG tube above the left hemidiaphragm with an abnormal U-shaped course or tip toward the left shoulder is a classic clue.
  • MRI: the diaphragm is a continuous low-signal band on T1- and T2-weighted imaging; MR signs parallel CT and MRI is generally reserved for stable patients.
  • Fluoroscopy: upper GI or barium enema may show a collar sign in delayed hernia but is rarely needed acutely.
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Congenital Bochdalek or Morgagni hernia: lacks trauma history and adjacent traumatic secondary signs.
  • Diaphragmatic eventration: thinned but continuous diaphragm remains attached to the costal margin; no focal defect, collar sign, or fallen viscus sign.
  • Paralyzed diaphragm: elevated but intact diaphragm without focal tear or herniation signs.
  • Pleural effusion or pulmonary/extrapleural mass may mimic the appearance on radiographs but should separate on CT.
🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Lateral blunt impact produces shear injury; frontal impact raises intraabdominal pressure and can rupture the diaphragm.
  • Diaphragmatic injuries do not heal spontaneously because of constant motion and the pressure gradient across the diaphragm.
  • If abdominal contents do not herniate immediately, negative intrapleural pressure can promote later herniation; positive-pressure ventilation may temporarily mask it.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Always inspect the diaphragm on trauma CT, especially when more obvious visceral injuries are present.
  • Right-sided injuries are more likely to be missed.
  • Contusion, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, atelectasis, and phrenic nerve palsy can obscure the injury.
  • Complications include obstruction or ischemia of herniated bowel, ischemia of herniated solid organs, respiratory compromise, and central venous obstruction; STATdx also describes tension gastrothorax.
📊 Key Measurements / Outcomes
  • Reported CT sensitivity may be as low as 73% and specificity as low as 50%.
  • Diaphragmatic injuries are missed in 7-66% of cases.
  • Associated injuries are reported in 52-100% of cases.
  • Overall mortality is reported by RadPrimer at 12-42%, largely from associated severe injuries; STATdx reports 30-60% mortality with delayed diagnosis and repair.
⭐ Super Summary
  • In trauma, think diaphragmatic rupture when abdominal viscera or fat are abnormally intrathoracic, especially with a collar sign, fallen/dependent viscus sign, or a focal diaphragm defect.
  • Use multiplanar CECT aggressively, and treat injuries above and below the diaphragm as a warning pattern even if the tear itself is subtle.

column11: Why does the fallen/dependent viscus sign occur after diaphragmatic rupture?

Imaging manifestation: this abnormal dependent contact is the fallen/dependent viscus sign.
Board discriminator: dependent posterior contact of abdominal viscera after trauma favors rupture over simple elevation with an intact diaphragm.

  • Diaphragmatic injuries do not heal spontaneously because of constant motion and the pressure gradient across the diaphragm.
  • If abdominal contents do not herniate immediately, negative intrapleural pressure can promote later herniation; positive-pressure ventilation may temporarily mask it.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Always inspect the diaphragm on trauma CT, especially when more obvious visceral injuries are present.
  • Right-sided injuries are more likely to be missed.
  • Contusion, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, atelectasis, and phrenic nerve palsy can obscure the injury.
  • Complications include obstruction or ischemia of herniated bowel, ischemia of herniated solid organs, respiratory compromise, and central venous obstruction; STATdx also describes tension gastrothorax.
📊 Key Measurements / Outcomes
  • Reported CT sensitivity may be as low as 73% and specificity as low as 50%.
  • Diaphragmatic injuries are missed in 7-66% of cases.
  • Associated injuries are reported in 52-100% of cases.
  • Overall mortality is reported by RadPrimer at 12-42%, largely from associated severe injuries; STATdx reports 30-60% mortality with delayed diagnosis and repair.
⭐ Super Summary
  • In trauma, think diaphragmatic rupture when abdominal viscera or fat are abnormally intrathoracic, especially with a collar sign, fallen/dependent viscus sign, or a focal diaphragm defect.
  • Use multiplanar CECT aggressively, and treat injuries above and below the diaphragm as a warning pattern even if the tear itself is subtle.
